The silver content of a Roman denarius dropped from about 4.4 grams of nearly pure silver at its launch in 211 BC down to nearly 0.1 (effectively silver-washed copper) by the late 3rd century AD which was a loss of 97.73% of its original value.  Since the passage of the 1913 Federal Reserve Act the Federal Reserve Note has lost 97.04% of its original purchasing power.  Notice how our Federal Reserve Note has essentially depreciated by the same percentage as the Roman denarius just prior to its collapse?

I understand everything Tom says. But this buying on the way down takes money, then more money. Where is this uninvested money sitting? At some point you have invested most, if not all, of what you have except the emergency fund. So at some point you are watching the value of your portfolio decrease without being able to add on and lower your average price. Lastly, I will add, how much does one need? Ex: I bought PLTR at 110 and sold it a few weeks ago at 168. I only had 100 shares so I only made 58 hundred dollars. Had I held on it would be closer to 10 K. Anyone care to wager that I won’t have the opportunity again to buy PLTR at 110? History is on my side. What does that mean? I would have lost 58 hundred dollars. I do it all the time. I don’t try to wring every dollar out of the market. I consistently make between 20 and 30 K a year doing what I just explained. The downside? TAXES. But I’m really uninterested in leaving money to people who did nothing to earn it so I can brag about how much money I have. People need to learn when enough is just fine. Oh, and I don’t need that 20 to 30 K to live on. I just look at my portfolio every January and enter the numbers into my spreadsheet. If the value goes up that much I consider it a very successful year.

Physical stacking will always be an integral part of my portfolio, but I've reached the point where I have all the physical metal I need to pass down. Lately, I've started funneling my usual physical purchases into gold and silver ETFs. The physical market spreads are just too extreme right now, and the daily liquidity of ETFs makes it so much easier to trade the volatility without dealing with shipping or insurance overhead. As an added bonus, it completely avoids the 10.6% Washington State tax on physical metals!
